disease_info: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is characterized by one or more major depressive episodes lasting at least two weeks, involving a persistent low mood or loss of interest along with associated cognitive, somatic, and behavioral changes that cause clinically significant distress or impairment. Typical features include changes in sleep, appetite or weight, energy, concentration, self-worth, and recurrent thoughts of death or suicide. The course can be single-episode or recurrent, with episodes often triggered by psychosocial stressors, medical illness, or occurring without clear precipitant, and may become chronic if untreated. MDD is distinguished from bipolar disorders by the absence of manic or hypomanic episodes and from normal grief by its pervasive impairment, self-critical or hopeless ruminations, and loss of capacity for pleasure that extends beyond culturally expected bereavement reactions.

narrative.personality: Daniel is a curious, hands-on, community-oriented retiree who thrives on spontaneous projects, social engagement, and learning new skills.
narrative.stressor: About two years ago, Daniel’s wife of nearly five decades died suddenly after a brief hospitalization, leaving him alone in the house where they had raised their children and built most of his cherished routines. Initially he coped by throwing himself into volunteer work, woodworking projects, and extra time at the senior center, telling himself that staying busy would keep the pain at bay. Over the following months, however, he began to reinterpret memories of their marriage through a harshly self-blaming lens, dwelling on arguments, missed opportunities, and the belief that he had failed her both emotionally and practically toward the end of her life. As this guilt deepened and colored his view of his past contributions to his family and community, he started withdrawing from the activities that once defined him, and his adult daughter finally persuaded him to see a psychiatrist after he confessed that he felt like a burden who had “wasted” his life and did not deserve the kindness others were showing him.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t stop thinking that my wife’s death is my fault and that I’ve been useless my whole life.”

narrative.personality: Mario is a quiet, meticulous, and thrifty man who finds comfort in routine, gardening, and solitary pastimes while remaining quietly devoted to his close-knit neighborhood.
narrative.stressor: Roughly two years ago, Mario underwent surgery and was diagnosed with a chronic cardiac condition that forced him to give up most of his handyman work and cut back on his long walks in Griffith Park. This health setback, coming on the heels of several years of widowhood, disrupted the carefully structured routines that had helped him feel useful and in control, and it left him increasingly preoccupied with his physical limitations and the fear of further decline. Over time he began spending more evenings alone at his kitchen table, poring over his expense ledger and worrying about becoming dependent on his children, while his once restorative gardening and neighborhood repairs felt more like exhausting obligations than sources of pride. As he grew more worn down and his nights became increasingly fragmented with long hours awake, his daughter urged him to seek psychiatric help after he admitted that he dreaded going to bed because he could no longer get a solid night’s sleep and felt he was “falling apart” without understanding why.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I just can’t sleep through the night anymore, no matter how tired I am.”

narrative.personality: Jason is an energetic, improvisational art professor who thrives on creative chaos, social connection, and exploring new cultural experiences.
narrative.stressor: Around two years ago, Jason’s department underwent a major restructuring, increasing his teaching load, adding administrative duties, and pressuring faculty to produce more traditional research output that clashed with his experimental, cross-disciplinary style. At the same time, a promising book project he had poured years into was rejected by several publishers with critiques that he interpreted as invalidating his entire intellectual approach. Initially he tried to respond in his usual fashion—taking on new side projects, volunteering for community workshops, and throwing himself into travel and social events—but the mounting demands and repeated professional disappointments gradually eroded his confidence in his academic judgment. Over the ensuing year and a half, preparing lectures and making routine academic decisions began to feel overwhelming rather than invigorating, and he finally agreed to see a psychiatrist after a close colleague noticed his growing difficulty organizing his thoughts in meetings and Jason admitted that he no longer trusted his own mind to make even simple choices about his work.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I can’t seem to think straight or make decisions about my work the way I used to.”
